_ui.disclaimer: This information is for educational purposes only and is not investment advice. Past performance does not guarantee future results. Data may be delayed or inaccurate.

price.label: Price
price.what: The latest price of one share.
price.how: Last traded price from the price provider. May be delayed.
price.good_bad: A price alone is not good or bad. Compare it with the company's earnings and history.

change_today.label: Change today
change_today.what: How much the price moved since yesterday's close.
change_today.how: Latest price minus previous close (and the same as a %).
change_today.good_bad: Daily moves are mostly noise. Moves above about 5% usually have news behind them.

market_cap.label: Market cap
market_cap.what: The total value of all the company's shares, i.e. what the market thinks the whole company is worth.
market_cap.how: Share price x number of shares outstanding.
market_cap.good_bad: Not good or bad. Large companies (over $10B) are usually more stable; small ones can grow faster but are riskier.

week52_range.label: 52-week range
week52_range.what: The lowest and highest price in the last year, and where today's price sits between them.
week52_range.how: Lowest daily low and highest daily high over the last 252 trading days.
week52_range.good_bad: Near the high = strong recent momentum but possibly expensive. Near the low = weak momentum, possibly cheap or in trouble.

next_earnings.label: Next earnings
next_earnings.what: The next date the company reports its quarterly results.
next_earnings.how: From the company's announced or expected earnings calendar.
next_earnings.good_bad: Prices often move a lot around earnings days. Know the date before you act.

shares_outstanding.label: Shares outstanding
shares_outstanding.what: How many shares of the company exist.
shares_outstanding.how: Reported by the company on the cover of its latest 10-Q or 10-K filing.
shares_outstanding.good_bad: A falling number (buybacks) is usually good for shareholders; a rising number (new shares) dilutes them.

data_freshness.label: Data freshness
data_freshness.what: The latest financial report the numbers come from.
data_freshness.how: Most recent 10-Q (quarterly) or 10-K (annual) filing on SEC EDGAR.
data_freshness.good_bad: Companies file every 3 months. A report older than about 4 months may mean a filing is late.

employees.label: Employees
employees.good_bad: Useful for scale. Revenue per employee helps compare efficiency between similar companies.

fiscal_year_end.label: Fiscal year end
fiscal_year_end.what: The day the company's financial year ends. Not always December 31.
fiscal_year_end.how: From the company's SEC registration data.
fiscal_year_end.good_bad: Not good or bad. It explains why, for example, Apple's 'Q1' is October to December.

sic_code.label: SIC code
sic_code.what: A government industry code the SEC uses to classify the company.
sic_code.how: From the company's SEC registration data.
sic_code.good_bad: Not good or bad. Useful to find similar companies.

ipo_date.label: IPO date
ipo_date.what: When the company's shares first started trading on the stock market.
ipo_date.how: From the data provider's company profile.
ipo_date.good_bad: Older listed companies have a longer track record to study.

revenue.label: Revenue
revenue.what: All the money the company earned from selling its products and services, before any costs.
revenue.good_bad: Steadily rising revenue is a good sign. Falling revenue for several quarters is a warning.

gross_profit.label: Gross profit
gross_profit.what: What is left from revenue after paying the direct cost of making the products.
gross_profit.good_bad: Higher is better. It shows pricing power. Banks and insurers don't have it.

operating_income.label: Operating income
operating_income.what: Profit from the core business, after running costs like R&D and marketing, before interest and tax.
operating_income.good_bad: Positive and growing is good. Negative means the core business loses money.

ebitda.label: EBITDA
ebitda.what: A rough measure of cash profit from operations, ignoring interest, taxes and non-cash write-downs.
ebitda.how: Operating income + depreciation & amortization (calculated by us).
ebitda.good_bad: Useful to compare companies with different debt. Not meaningful for banks and insurers.

net_income.label: Net income
net_income.what: The final profit after all costs, interest and taxes. The 'bottom line'.
net_income.good_bad: Positive and growing is good. One-off items can make a single quarter look unusual.

eps_diluted.label: EPS (diluted, GAAP)
eps_diluted.what: Profit per share: how much of the net income belongs to each share.
eps_diluted.how: Net income / diluted share count (official GAAP number).
eps_diluted.good_bad: Growing EPS is good. Note: analysts often quote an 'adjusted' EPS that can differ.

margins.label: Profit margins
margins.what: How many cents of each $1 of revenue are kept as profit, at each level of the income statement.
margins.how: Gross, operating, EBITDA or net profit / revenue.
margins.good_bad: Higher and rising margins are good. Compare with similar companies: software has higher margins than retail.

growth.label: Growth vs last year
growth.what: How much revenue and EPS changed compared with the same period one year earlier.
growth.how: (This period / same period last year) - 1. Comparing the same quarter removes seasonal effects.
growth.good_bad: Positive is good. Steady growth is usually better than big swings.

expense_breakdown.label: Expense breakdown
expense_breakdown.what: How the company spends its revenue: making products (COGS), research (R&D), and selling/admin (SG&A).
expense_breakdown.good_bad: Falling percentages mean the company is getting more efficient.

total_assets.label: Total assets
total_assets.what: Everything the company owns: cash, buildings, inventory, investments.
total_assets.how: Reported in the balance sheet. Always equals liabilities + equity.
total_assets.good_bad: Not good or bad alone. Compare it with what the company owes.

total_debt.label: Total debt
total_debt.what: All borrowed money the company must repay.
total_debt.good_bad: Lower is safer. Debt is fine if profits easily cover the interest.

net_debt.label: Net debt
net_debt.what: Debt left over if the company used all its cash to repay it.
net_debt.good_bad: Negative net debt (more cash than debt) is a very strong position.

current_ratio.label: Current ratio
current_ratio.what: Can the company pay bills due within a year using assets it can turn into cash within a year?
current_ratio.good_bad: Above 1.5 is comfortable. Below 1.0 can be a warning (except for very strong companies like Apple).

debt_to_equity.label: Debt to equity
debt_to_equity.what: How much the company borrows compared with the money owned by shareholders.
debt_to_equity.good_bad: Below 1.0 is generally conservative; above 2.0 is high. Large buybacks can make equity small and this ratio look high.

operating_cash_flow.label: Operating cash flow
operating_cash_flow.what: Actual cash generated by the business (not accounting profit).
operating_cash_flow.how: Reported in the cash flow statement. 10-Q filings report it year-to-date, so we subtract to get single quarters.
operating_cash_flow.good_bad: Positive and above net income is a sign of high-quality earnings.

capex.label: Capital expenditure (capex)
capex.what: Cash spent on buildings, equipment and other long-term assets.
capex.how: Reported in the cash flow statement.
capex.good_bad: Needed to grow, but very high capex leaves less cash for shareholders.

fcf.label: Free cash flow (FCF)
fcf.what: Cash left after running and investing in the business. This can pay dividends, buy back shares or repay debt.
fcf.good_bad: Positive and growing is very good. Negative FCF for a long time is a warning.

shareholder_returns.label: Shareholder returns
shareholder_returns.what: Cash the company gave back to shareholders.
shareholder_returns.how: Dividends paid + money spent buying back its own shares.
shareholder_returns.good_bad: Steady returns are good if they are paid from free cash flow, not new debt.

derived.label: Derived values (✱)
derived.what: Numbers we calculated because the company doesn't report them directly.
derived.how: Q4 = full year minus Q1 to Q3. Quarterly cash flow = year-to-date minus the previous year-to-date.
derived.good_bad: They are exact for most items. Q4 EPS and share counts are close approximations.

pe.label: P/E (TTM)
pe.what: How many dollars investors pay for each $1 of yearly profit.
pe.how: Share price / earnings per share of the last 12 months. N/A when earnings are negative.
pe.good_bad: Lower can mean cheaper, higher means investors expect more growth. Compare with the stock's own history and its peers.

forward_pe.label: Forward P/E
forward_pe.what: Like P/E, but using analysts' profit estimate for the next fiscal year.
forward_pe.how: Share price / expected EPS for the next fiscal year (analyst estimate).
forward_pe.good_bad: Lower than today's P/E means profits are expected to grow. Estimates can be wrong.

peg.label: PEG
peg.how: P/E / expected yearly EPS growth in % (uses analyst estimates).
peg.good_bad: Around 1 is often seen as fair; below 1 can be cheap for its growth; above 2 expensive.

ps.label: P/S (TTM)
ps.what: How much investors pay for each $1 of yearly sales.
ps.how: Market cap / revenue of the last 12 months.
ps.good_bad: Useful when profits are small or negative. High-margin businesses usually have higher P/S.

pb.label: P/B
pb.what: Price compared with the company's accounting net worth (book value).
pb.good_bad: Most useful for banks and insurers (around 1-2 is typical). Big buybacks can make P/B very high for tech companies.

ev_ebitda.label: EV/EBITDA
ev_ebitda.what: Price of the whole business (including debt) compared with its operating cash profit.
ev_ebitda.how: Enterprise value / EBITDA of the last 12 months.
ev_ebitda.good_bad: Lower is cheaper. Around 10 is common for mature companies. Not meaningful for banks.

ev_revenue.label: EV/Revenue
ev_revenue.what: Price of the whole business (including debt) compared with its yearly sales.
ev_revenue.how: Enterprise value / revenue of the last 12 months.
ev_revenue.good_bad: Lower is cheaper; compare with similar companies.

p_fcf.label: P/FCF
p_fcf.what: How much investors pay for each $1 of yearly free cash flow.
p_fcf.how: Market cap / free cash flow of the last 12 months.
p_fcf.good_bad: Below about 20 is often considered reasonable; very high means investors expect strong growth.

fcf_yield.label: FCF yield
fcf_yield.what: Free cash flow as a percentage of the company's market value. Like an 'interest rate' the business earns for owners.
fcf_yield.good_bad: Higher is better. Above about 5% is attractive; negative means the company burns cash.

earnings_yield.label: Earnings yield
earnings_yield.what: Profit as a percentage of the share price: the inverse of P/E.
earnings_yield.good_bad: Compare with bond yields: a stock earning less than safe bonds needs strong growth to be worth it.

enterprise_value.label: Enterprise value (EV)
enterprise_value.what: The price to buy the whole company, including its debt, minus its cash.
enterprise_value.how: Market cap + total debt - cash and short-term investments.
enterprise_value.good_bad: Not good or bad alone; used in EV/EBITDA and EV/Revenue.

target_upside.label: Analyst target upside
target_upside.what: How far the average Wall Street analyst price target is above or below today's price.
target_upside.how: (Mean analyst price target / price) - 1. Third-party opinion, not our view.
target_upside.good_bad: Targets are often wrong and change often. Treat as one opinion, not a forecast.

roe.label: ROE (return on equity)
roe.what: How much profit the company makes with the money owned by shareholders.
roe.good_bad: Above 15% is generally strong. Very high ROE can come from large debt or buybacks (small equity).

roa.label: ROA (return on assets)
roa.what: How much profit the company makes from everything it owns.
roa.how: Net income (TTM) / average total assets. (Yahoo uses a slightly different formula, so numbers can differ.)
roa.good_bad: Above 5% is good for most companies; banks are usually around 1%.

roic.label: ROIC (return on invested capital)
roic.what: Profit from operations compared with all the money invested in the business (by lenders and owners).
roic.how: NOPAT / (debt + equity - cash). NOPAT = operating income x (1 - tax rate).
roic.good_bad: Above about 10-15% means the company creates value. Not meaningful for banks.

dupont.label: DuPont breakdown
dupont.what: Splits ROE into three drivers: profitability, efficiency and leverage (debt).
dupont.how: ROE = net margin x asset turnover (revenue / assets) x equity multiplier (assets / equity).
dupont.good_bad: ROE driven by margin and turnover is healthier than ROE driven mostly by debt.

effective_tax_rate.label: Effective tax rate
effective_tax_rate.what: The share of pretax profit paid as income tax.
effective_tax_rate.good_bad: The US federal rate is 21%. Very low rates may not last.

cagr.label: CAGR (compound annual growth)
cagr.what: The average yearly growth rate over several years.
cagr.how: (Last value / first value)^(1 / years) - 1, from annual reports.
cagr.good_bad: Higher is better. N/A when a start or end value is negative.

bvps.label: Book value per share
bvps.what: The company's accounting net worth per share.
bvps.good_bad: Growing book value is good. Compare with price using P/B.

quick_ratio.label: Quick ratio
quick_ratio.what: Like the current ratio, but without inventory (which can be hard to sell fast).

debt_to_ebitda.label: Debt to EBITDA
debt_to_ebitda.what: How many years of operating cash profit it would take to repay all debt.
debt_to_ebitda.good_bad: Below 2 is comfortable, above 4 is high.

interest_coverage.label: Interest coverage
interest_coverage.what: How many times operating profit covers the interest on debt.
interest_coverage.good_bad: Above 5x is comfortable; below 2x is risky.

cash_conversion.label: Cash conversion
cash_conversion.what: How much of the reported profit actually arrives as cash.
cash_conversion.good_bad: Around 1.0 or higher is healthy. Far below 1 for a long time can be a warning about earnings quality.

valuation_history.label: Valuation history
valuation_history.what: How expensive the stock was on each day of the last 5 years.
valuation_history.how: Daily price vs the 12-month earnings/sales known on that day (using filing dates, so no future data is used).
valuation_history.good_bad: Above the median line = more expensive than usual; below = cheaper than usual. History doesn't have to repeat.

peers.label: Peer comparison
peers.what: The same ratios for similar companies.
peers.how: Peer list from Finnhub; peer ratios from Yahoo Finance (demo data). Peer median = middle value.
peers.good_bad: Being cheaper than peers can mean a bargain or a weaker business. Look at growth and margins too.

graham.label: Graham number
graham.what: A classic, very conservative 'fair price' formula by Benjamin Graham.
graham.how: Square root of 22.5 x EPS x book value per share. Estimate, not a prediction.
graham.good_bad: Built for stable, asset-heavy companies. Most growth companies trade far above it.

dcf.label: DCF (discounted cash flow)
dcf.what: An estimate of value from the cash the business might generate in the future.
dcf.how: Project free cash flow 5 years, add a terminal value, discount back to today, subtract net debt, divide by shares.
dcf.good_bad: Very sensitive to the assumptions. Use it to understand what the price implies, not as a prediction.

piotroski.label: Piotroski F-score
piotroski.what: A 0-9 checklist of financial strength: profitability, debt, and efficiency, each compared with the year before.
piotroski.how: One point for each of 9 tests passed, using annual SEC data.
piotroski.good_bad: 7-9 is strong, 4-6 is average, 0-3 is weak.

altman.label: Altman Z-score
altman.what: A formula that estimates the risk of financial distress (bankruptcy) within about 2 years.
altman.how: 1.2 x working capital/assets + 1.4 x retained earnings/assets + 3.3 x EBIT/assets + 0.6 x market cap/liabilities + 1.0 x sales/assets.
altman.good_bad: Above 2.99 = safe zone, 1.81-2.99 = grey zone, below 1.81 = distress zone. Not used for banks and insurers.

price_chart.label: Price chart
price_chart.what: Each candle shows one day: the body runs from open to close (green = closed higher, red = closed lower), the thin lines show the day's high and low.
price_chart.how: Daily prices. Panels below: trading volume, RSI and MACD.
price_chart.good_bad: Charts show what happened, not what will happen.

sma.label: Moving averages (SMA 20 / 50 / 200)
sma.what: The average closing price of the last 20, 50 or 200 trading days. Smooths out daily noise to show the trend.
sma.how: Sum of the last N closing prices / N.
sma.good_bad: Price above the 200-day average is commonly read as a long-term uptrend; below as a downtrend.

rsi.label: RSI (14)
rsi.what: Measures how fast and how much the price moved recently, on a 0-100 scale.
rsi.how: Wilder's formula: 100 - 100 / (1 + average gain / average loss) over 14 days.
rsi.good_bad: Above 70 = 'overbought zone' (rose fast), below 30 = 'oversold zone' (fell fast). Strong trends can stay there for a long time.

macd.label: MACD (12, 26, 9)
macd.what: Shows changes in momentum by comparing a fast and a slow moving average.
macd.how: MACD = 12-day EMA - 26-day EMA. Signal = 9-day EMA of MACD. Histogram = MACD - signal.
macd.good_bad: MACD crossing above the signal line = momentum turning up; below = turning down. Many false signals in sideways markets.

bollinger.label: Bollinger Bands (20, 2)
bollinger.what: A band around the 20-day average that widens when prices are volatile and narrows when calm.
bollinger.good_bad: Touching a band shows a big move relative to recent volatility, not a reversal by itself.

atr.label: ATR (14)
atr.what: The average daily price range (how much the stock typically moves in a day).
atr.how: Average of the 'true range' over 14 days (Wilder smoothing).
atr.good_bad: Higher ATR = bigger daily swings = more risk. Shown also as % of price.

volume.label: Volume vs average
volume.what: How many shares traded today compared with a normal day.
volume.good_bad: Above 1.5x means unusual interest, often around news or earnings.

support_resistance.label: Support and resistance
support_resistance.what: Price areas where the stock turned around before. Support is below the price, resistance above.
support_resistance.how: Find swing highs and lows (5 days each side) plus the window's highest high and lowest low, group prices within max(0.5 x ATR, 1.5%), rank by number of touches (recent and high-volume touches count more).
support_resistance.good_bad: Support and resistance are areas where price reacted before. They are not guarantees.

pivots.label: Pivot points (weekly)
pivots.what: Reference levels for this week calculated from last week's high, low and close.
pivots.how: P = (High + Low + Close) / 3; R1 = 2P - Low; S1 = 2P - High; R2 = P + (High - Low); S2 = P - (High - Low).
pivots.good_bad: Many short-term traders watch them, which is why price sometimes reacts there. Not guarantees.

trend_signals.label: Trend signals
trend_signals.what: Simple facts about the current trend, with the date they happened.
trend_signals.how: Price vs 50/200-day averages, golden/death cross (50-day crossing the 200-day) in the last 60 days, RSI zone, MACD crossover.
trend_signals.good_bad: Facts, not advice. Signals often contradict each other.

returns.label: Returns
returns.what: How much the stock gained or lost over each period, compared with the market (SPY) and its sector ETF.
returns.how: Price at the end / price at the start - 1, using prices adjusted for dividends and splits.
returns.good_bad: Beating the market over 1-5 years is a good sign; short periods are mostly noise.

relative_performance.label: Relative performance
relative_performance.what: The stock, the market (SPY) and its sector ETF, all starting at 100, so you can compare them directly.
relative_performance.how: Each line = price / price on the first day x 100 (dividend-adjusted).
relative_performance.good_bad: A rising gap above SPY means the stock beat the market over the period.

beta.label: Beta
beta.what: How much the stock tends to move when the market moves.
beta.how: From 2 years of weekly returns: covariance(stock, SPY) / variance(SPY).
beta.good_bad: 1.0 = moves like the market; 1.5 = 50% bigger swings; below 1 = calmer than the market.

volatility.label: Volatility (1 year)
volatility.what: How much the price bounces around, expressed per year.
volatility.how: Standard deviation of daily returns over 1 year x square root of 252.
volatility.good_bad: Below 20% is calm, 20-40% typical for single stocks, above 50% very volatile.

max_drawdown.label: Maximum drawdown
max_drawdown.what: The biggest fall from a peak to a later low in the period.
max_drawdown.how: Lowest value of (price / highest price so far - 1).
max_drawdown.good_bad: Shows the pain an investor could have felt. -20% is common; -50% or worse is severe.

sharpe.label: Sharpe ratio (1 year)
sharpe.what: Return earned per unit of risk taken, above a risk-free investment.
sharpe.good_bad: Above 1 is good, above 2 very good, below 0 means a T-bill did better.

monthly_returns.label: Monthly returns
monthly_returns.what: The return of each calendar month, to spot seasonal patterns.
monthly_returns.good_bad: Patterns in the past may not repeat.

drawdown.label: Drawdown chart
drawdown.what: How far below its previous high the stock was on each day.
drawdown.good_bad: Deep and long 'underwater' periods show how risky the stock has been.

eps_surprise.label: EPS actual vs expected
eps_surprise.what: Compares the profit per share the company reported with what Wall Street analysts expected.
eps_surprise.how: Surprise % = (reported EPS - average analyst estimate) / |estimate|. Beat = above +1%, miss = below -1%, otherwise inline. 'Reported EPS' is usually the adjusted (non-GAAP) number analysts track.
eps_surprise.good_bad: Regular beats suggest the company sets beatable expectations or is doing better than expected. The price reaction matters as much as the beat itself.

beat_rate.label: Beat rate
beat_rate.what: How often the company beat analysts' EPS estimates.
beat_rate.how: Number of beats / number of quarters (last 8 and last 12).
beat_rate.good_bad: Most large US companies beat about 70-80% of the time, so a high beat rate is normal; a low one stands out.

earnings_reaction.label: Post-earnings price move
earnings_reaction.what: How much the stock moved right after each earnings report.
earnings_reaction.how: From the last close BEFORE the market could react (previous close if reported before the open; same-day close if after the close) to the close 1 day and 5 days later.
earnings_reaction.good_bad: 'Typical earnings move' (average absolute 1-day move) shows how much risk an earnings day usually brings.

gaap_vs_adjusted.label: GAAP EPS vs reported (adjusted) EPS
gaap_vs_adjusted.what: GAAP EPS is the official number in the SEC filing. 'Reported' EPS from data providers is usually adjusted, excluding one-off items.
gaap_vs_adjusted.how: GAAP diluted EPS from SEC EDGAR; reported EPS from yfinance.
gaap_vs_adjusted.good_bad: A big, lasting gap (adjusted much higher than GAAP) deserves a closer look at what is being excluded.

estimate_revisions.label: Estimate revisions
estimate_revisions.what: How analysts' EPS estimates changed over the last 90 days.
estimate_revisions.how: Average analyst estimate now vs 7, 30, 60 and 90 days ago, plus the number of analysts who raised or lowered their estimate.
estimate_revisions.good_bad: Rising estimates usually mean business is going better than expected; falling estimates the opposite.

upcoming_earnings.label: Upcoming earnings
upcoming_earnings.what: The next scheduled earnings report and what analysts expect.
upcoming_earnings.how: Date and analyst averages from data providers. Dates can change until the company confirms them.
upcoming_earnings.good_bad: Prices often move a lot around earnings. Know the date and the expectations.

revenue_surprise.label: Revenue actual vs expected
revenue_surprise.what: Reported revenue (from the SEC filing) compared with the analyst estimate, where an estimate is available.
revenue_surprise.how: Actual revenue from SEC EDGAR; estimates from Finnhub (free data covers only the most recent quarter).
revenue_surprise.good_bad: Beating on revenue shows real demand; beating only on EPS can come from cost cuts or lower taxes.

dividend_yield.label: Dividend yield (TTM)
dividend_yield.what: The yearly cash dividend as a percentage of the share price.
dividend_yield.how: Dividends per share paid in the last 12 months / current price.
dividend_yield.good_bad: 2-4% is typical for mature companies. A very high yield can be a warning that the market expects a cut.

payout_ratio.label: Payout ratio
payout_ratio.what: The share of profit paid out as dividends.
payout_ratio.how: Dividends paid (last 12 months) / net income (last 12 months), from SEC filings.
payout_ratio.good_bad: Below about 60% is comfortable; above 100% means the company pays more than it earns, which can't last.

fcf_payout.label: FCF payout ratio
fcf_payout.what: The share of free cash flow paid out as dividends: dividends are paid from cash, not profit.
fcf_payout.good_bad: Below about 70% leaves room to keep raising the dividend.

dividend_growth.label: Dividend growth
dividend_growth.what: How fast the dividend per share has grown, and for how many years in a row it was raised.
dividend_growth.how: CAGR of yearly dividends per share (3 and 5 years). Streak = consecutive calendar years in which the regular dividend was raised (special one-off dividends ignored). Based on Yahoo's dividend history; very old records can be incomplete, so long streaks may be undercounted.
dividend_growth.good_bad: A long streak (25+ years = 'dividend aristocrat') shows a strong commitment to the dividend.

ex_dividend.label: Ex-dividend date
ex_dividend.what: You must own the shares BEFORE this date to receive the next dividend.
ex_dividend.good_bad: The price usually drops by about the dividend amount on this date.

holders.label: Who owns the shares
holders.what: How the shares are split between company insiders, institutions (funds, pensions) and everyone else.
holders.how: Latest filings collected by Yahoo Finance.
holders.good_bad: High institutional ownership means professional investors are involved; meaningful insider ownership aligns management with shareholders.

insiders.label: Insider transactions
insiders.what: Shares bought or sold by the company's own directors and officers (reported on SEC Form 4).
insiders.how: Purchases and sales by month. Stock awards, gifts and option exercises are listed but not counted as buys or sells.
insiders.good_bad: Insiders sell for many reasons (taxes, diversification). Open-market buying is rarer and more meaningful.

analyst_ratings.label: Wall Street analysts' ratings
analyst_ratings.what: How many Wall Street analysts rate the stock 'buy', 'hold' or 'sell'. This is a third-party opinion, not ours.
analyst_ratings.how: Monthly counts from data providers (Finnhub first, then Yahoo).
analyst_ratings.good_bad: Analysts are often too optimistic and change views late. Use ratings as one input, not a decision.

short_interest.label: Short interest
short_interest.what: Shares sold short by investors betting the price will fall.
short_interest.how: % of float = shares sold short / shares available to trade. Days to cover = shares short / average daily volume.
short_interest.good_bad: Below 5% of float is normal; above 20% means many investors are betting against the stock (and sharp 'short squeezes' are possible).

news.label: News
news.what: Recent articles about the company from news providers.
news.how: Finnhub company news first, then Yahoo Finance. Duplicate headlines removed.
news.good_bad: Headlines are not verified by us. Read the original article and check the official SEC filings.

sec_filings.label: SEC filings
sec_filings.what: The company's official reports to the US regulator.
sec_filings.how: 10-K = annual report, 10-Q = quarterly report, 8-K = important event (e.g. earnings), Form 4 = insider trade.
sec_filings.good_bad: The most reliable source: what the company must legally disclose.
